::: {.oneline}
A photon is one unit of energy in one particular vibration pattern of the
electromagnetic field. It is a property of the field, and not an object flying
through it.
:::

## Short answer

The electromagnetic field can vibrate in many independent patterns at the same
time, differing in direction, wavelength and polarization. Quantum mechanics
tells us that the energy stored in any one of these patterns cannot take
arbitrary values: it climbs in equal steps, whose size is fixed by the rate at
which that pattern oscillates. A photon is one such step.

This is the entire content of the word. A photon carries an energy, a direction
and a polarization, since the vibration pattern does. It does not carry a
position, since a vibration pattern is spread over the whole region in which the
field lives. Asking where a photon is, is therefore close to asking where the
note middle C is inside a piano.

We also use the same word for something rather different, namely the click of a
detector. That click is real, and it is discrete, but its discreteness comes
from the detector (from an atom in it absorbing a fixed amount of energy) and
not from the field. Most of the time the two meanings agree closely enough that
nobody minds. Occasionally they come apart, and it then matters which of the two
we had in mind.

## Why it works this way

Nothing about a vibrating field requires its energy to come in steps. What
requires it is the experimental fact that matter exchanges energy with light in
fixed amounts proportional to frequency, the photoelectric effect being the
best known case. Quantizing the field is thus the bookkeeping that makes this
fact automatic rather than mysterious.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: from Maxwell to a ladder

Expanding the free field in plane-wave modes in a volume $V$ and substituting
into the field energy, the cross terms between different modes integrate away
and what is left is a sum of independent harmonic oscillators:

$$
\hat H = \sum_{\mathbf k \lambda} \hbar\omega_{\mathbf k}
\left( \hat a^\dagger_{\mathbf k \lambda}\hat a_{\mathbf k \lambda}
+ \tfrac{1}{2} \right)
$$ {#eq-field-hamiltonian}

with $[\hat a_{\mathbf k\lambda}, \hat a^\dagger_{\mathbf k'\lambda'}]
= \delta_{\mathbf k\mathbf k'}\delta_{\lambda\lambda'}$. The state
$\hat a^\dagger_{\mathbf k\lambda}\lvert 0\rangle$ carries one more quantum in
mode $(\mathbf k,\lambda)$, with energy $\hbar\omega_{\mathbf k}$, momentum
$\hbar\mathbf k$ and polarization $\lambda$.

Plane waves are a convenience and not a necessity. Any complete set of solutions
of the free wave equation defines modes, and therefore defines what counts as
one photon. Photon number is basis dependent in precisely this sense.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why there is no photon wavefunction

Localizing the field arbitrarily sharply costs unbounded energy and mixes the
positive and negative frequency parts of the field, so that no position operator
with the usual properties exists. The closest useful object is the
photon-detection amplitude, which is a statement about the field where the
detector sits, and not about where a particle was beforehand.
:::

## Common confusions

- **"A photon is a little packet travelling from source to detector."**
  Vibration patterns are spread out. Whatever localization an experiment shows
  comes from the geometry of the source and of the detector.
- **"A laser emits photons one at a time."** A laser emits a state that is a
  superposition of all photon numbers at once, as discussed in
  [why a classical field requires coherence](../classical-field-coherence/index.qmd).
- **"The number of photons is a fact about the field."** It depends on the set
  of vibration patterns we have chosen to count in, and for an accelerating
  observer even on the observer.
